title: What you will be able to do
instruction: Press reveal to see each outcome for this lesson.

_items.text: Recognise analysis as breaking an interpretation, body of evidence or data set down through close examination.

title: Analysis is not summary
body: At intermediate level, 'critical thinking' stops being one word for everything and splits into skills you can name and practise separately. The first of these is analysis.

title: What analysis actually means
body: Dennis and Abbott (2026, pp.119-120) define it directly: 'Analysis refers to the breaking down or opening up of an interpretation, a body of evidence, or a data set through close examination.' Analysis is not describing what a source says. It is taking that claim apart to see what it is built on.

title: Worked example
body:
Consider two students reading the same journal article.

{{learner-a}} reads a scholar's interpretation and summarises it accurately in their own words.

{{learner-b}} reads the same interpretation and breaks it into its claim, the evidence offered for it, and the assumption it rests on.

Both could restate the interpretation. Only {{learner-b}} had analysed it.

title: Why this is a distinct skill
body: A good summary can still leave an interpretation untouched. Analysis means opening it up: separating the claim from the evidence from the assumption, so each part can be checked on its own.

definition: The breaking down or opening up of an interpretation, a body of evidence, or a data set through close examination (Dennis and Abbott, 2026, p.119).
extendedDefinition: Analysis is the skill this lesson isolates from the wider idea of 'being critical': it is one specific move, not the whole habit.
example: Analysing an argument means separating its claim from the evidence it rests on, rather than simply repeating the claim.

title: Order the steps of analysis
displayTitle: Put the steps of analysing an interpretation in order
body: These four steps describe how to analyse an interpretation, but they are out of sequence.
instruction: Drag items to reorder, or use the keyboard (Enter to grab, arrows to move, Enter to drop). Then select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Put the four steps of analysis in order, from first to last.

_items.text: Identify the evidence offered for it.
Identify the assumption it rests on.
Decide what the claim actually depends on.

_feedback.correct: That is the right order. You need the claim and its evidence before you can see the assumption underneath, and only then can you say what it depends on.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what you need to see before you can spot the assumption underneath a claim.

title: Practising analysis on your own reading
body: Next time you read an interpretation for a seminar, try writing its claim, its evidence, and its assumption as three separate lines. If you cannot fill in all three, you have found where the interpretation is thin.

title: Your turn
instruction: This is for your own reflection; no right answers are expected.

_items.text: Pick a claim from something you read this week. What was its evidence, and what assumption sat underneath it?
Was there a claim you accepted without being able to state its evidence? What made you accept it anyway?
